turns.text:
I'm angry and honestly a little hurt. Saturday a database migration we ran failed and bookings were down 3 hours 41 minutes. Delphine, one of our biggest customers, posted about it on LinkedIn at 1:15. My co-founder Mariana wrote in our founders' channel that she was calling Delphine at 4 and wanted to hold off on any public reply until then.

By 2:30 the post had 64 comments, and other studio owners, three of them our customers, were asking whether we'd said anything at all. After our March outage we wrote a rule together: a public complaint gets a public reply within an hour. So at 2:35 I posted a plain answer. I apologized, said what broke, gave the downtime, noted our status updates from 8:40, and promised a write-up Monday. Two studio owners thanked me for the straight answer.

Then I find out Mariana had told Delphine it looked like our hosting provider. It wasn't, and I'd corrected that in the incident channel at 10:30. Now she's treating my comment like sabotage. I think she cares more about looking in control than about getting it right.

Our founders' meeting is Monday at 9:30. How do I bring this up with her tomorrow?

You have good reasons to be upset. You followed a rule you both wrote, your reply was accurate, and the people reading it appreciated it. But if you go in trying to prove you were right, Monday becomes a trial. A better goal is to fix what's broken: Delphine has been told the wrong cause, and your rule clearly doesn't cover what happens when one founder asks to hold off.

(Quick check: today is Monday the 12th. If the meeting is this morning, you have less prep time than you think, and the write-up you promised is due today too.)

## Before you talk to her

**Find out whether she saw your 10:30 correction.** If she was busy preparing for the Delphine call and missed it, she didn't knowingly tell a customer something false. She was working from old information. That changes the whole conversation, so ask instead of assuming.

**Be honest with yourself about your part.** She asked in the founders' channel to wait until 4. You posted at 2:35 without replying to her first. You had good reasons: 64 comments, customers asking, and your agreed rule. But from her side, she made a clear request and you overrode it without a word, and then her call with Delphine went sideways. That's why it feels like sabotage to her. The fix would have been one line to her at 2:20: "Comments are piling up, customers are asking. I'm posting a short factual reply at 2:35 per our rule unless you object."

**Drop the line about her caring more about looking in control.** You may believe it, but saying it guarantees a fight about her character instead of a fix.

## How to open

Start with your own part, then the shared problem:

> "I want to talk about Saturday. First, I should have told you before I posted. You asked us to hold, and I went ahead without a word. I'm sorry about that. I posted because the thread was at 64 comments, three of our customers were asking if we'd said anything, and our March rule says one hour. But I get why it felt like I went around you."

Then raise the bigger issue as something you both have to solve:

> "The bigger problem is that Delphine heard 'hosting provider' and the public thread says it was our migration. Did you see my 10:30 update in the incident channel? Either way, she has the wrong picture, and we need to fix that before the write-up goes out."

## What to settle in the meeting

1. **Correcting things with Delphine.** Mariana should probably make that call, since it was her conversation. Offer to join or help. Do it before the write-up publishes so Delphine doesn't learn the real cause from a blog post.
2. **The write-up.** Agree on who writes it, who reviews it, and when it ships. Make the root cause unambiguous.
3. **A gap in the rule.** "Public reply within an hour" doesn't cover a founder asking to hold off. Agree on something like: either founder can ask for a delay, but past the hour, a short factual acknowledgment goes out regardless, and the poster gives the other a heads-up first.
4. **One source of truth during incidents.** Before anyone tells a customer the cause, they check the incident channel. This would have prevented Saturday.

## If she stays angry

Don't argue over whether your post was the right call. Keep coming back to what you both want: "We both want Delphine to stay, and we both want customers to trust us. What would have worked better for you Saturday?" Her answer will tell you whether this was about being blindsided, or about something deeper you two need to sort out.

You can hold your ground on the substance, since you were accurate and on time, and still own the part where you left her out.

On the main questions, yes. You followed the rule you both agreed to, your post was accurate, and customers were asking. A plain, correct answer was the right call, and the reactions back that up. Mariana telling Delphine it was the hosting provider is the actual problem from Saturday, whatever the reason.

On how you did it, not entirely. She asked in writing to hold, and you posted without replying to her. A one-line heads-up would have cost you nothing and kept her from walking into the Delphine call blind. That doesn't make your post wrong. It makes her reaction understandable.

And "she cares more about looking in control than getting it right" is a guess about her motives. It might be true, but you don't know yet, especially if she missed your 10:30 correction.

So you were right about what to say and when. You were wrong to skip the heads-up. If you open Monday by owning the second, you'll have a much easier time getting her to agree on the first.
